questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: It was many-fold. First and foremost, I wanted to go on exchange in an English speaking country, which reduced the number of options. Secondly, I wanted to visit a country too far away to visit on a smaller vacation. After picking a country I looked for a large city with a good university.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. Their student administration Stop 1 works very smoothly.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I needed to get a student ID and enroll in other courses than I had initially planned.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Most of those who became my friends arrived without having found a place and then surveyed the different areas for a couple of weeks. Everyone found something in the end.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Check out the Facebook group Fairy Floss Real Estate; it has 400k members and there are frequent posts about housing. That site, and the Flatmates website should be the main two ways of finding housing in Melbourne.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It takes some time to find good housing, so if possible I recommend arriving a couple of weeks before the semester starts. Also be careful not to get scammed.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You enroll in courses online. It was a bit tiresome as a postgradute student because you have to contact various Lecturers and have them accept that you live up to the course prerequisites.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Unimelb course handbook and Stop 1.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Somewhat succesful. I had a lot of overlaps. Luckily, you can change your courses until quite late in the semester.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Enroll in more subjects than 30 ECTS and then go to different courses and check them out.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The Bachelor's courses very comparable to or easier than Bachelor's courses on UCPH. The Master's/Honor's courses very comparable to or perhaps slightly tougher than similar courses on UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Very comparable. The only difference might be that assignments and mid-semester tests count towards your final grade on Unimelb.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Positive Political Economics (ECON40009 or ECON90037)
Econometrics of Markets and Competition (ECOM90017)
Experimental Economics (ECON30022)
Elements of Data Processing (COMP20008)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend all my courses except Experimental Economics. Unless you want a very easy, but quite dull course. Teaching was not great either.
Positive Political Economics was a tough, but extremely rewarding, theoretical course, but Eik Swee (The lecturer) has a challenging way of teaching, where he forces students to think hard about the questions he put forth before answering them. 
As Aaron, the Lecturer in Econometrics of Markets and Competition said: you cannot find many courses like this where it is not a PhD course. It had a quite large workload in terms of assignments. But you learn Matlab from scratch and learn how to estimate advanced structurcal models with heterogenous agents.
Elements of Data Processing was comparatively easier course if you have any experience using Python. Half of the course was in Machine Learning which was why I picked it.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had to live in a hostel both in the start of and the end of my visit, which costs more per month than the other housing I found.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Others payed way more for housing than me, but I had an hour of transportation each way to and from Uni.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Did not participate in them.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a very good fitness on campus, which is cheaper than working out in other gyms in the city.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Sign up for Foodrelief. It is a program where you can receive free frozen meals once a week.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Plan on spending a month or two before or after the semester where you go travelling. The West Coast, the East Coast, Grampians, Wilsons Prom, Phillip Island, Mornington Peninsula, Great Ocean Road, Uluru (Ayer's Rock)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Yes, I mostly spend time with Danish people.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: No. My best guess is that around 80 percent of the students in Economics and Business are Asian people so there is quite a big cultural barrier.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Australians are very relaxed and down to earth. If you have an open mind you can easily end up in a conversation on a bar, café etc.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Save enough money and plan on going travelling before or after the semester.
2. Foodrelief and Fairy Floss Real Estate.
3. Socialise with other Danish people from UCPH after you know where you are going. If you do not link up with locals it provides another nice way of having a semester abroad.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting better at English, living in a country far from friends and family.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The exam period. Because I did not study that hard during the semester I had a lot of catching up to do.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
